bio-oxygen-dissociation.title: The oxygen dissociation curve and the Bohr shift
bio-oxygen-dissociation.caption: In the lungs haemoglobin is almost fully saturated. In respiring tissue, where pO₂ is low, the steep middle of the curve means a small fall in pO₂ releases a lot of oxygen. More CO₂ shifts the curve right (lower affinity), so even more is released; fetal haemoglobin's curve lies to the left (higher affinity).
bio-oxygen-dissociation.alt: S-shaped oxygen dissociation curves of percentage saturation against partial pressure of oxygen, with the curve for high carbon dioxide shifted right and fetal haemoglobin shifted left.
description: The horizontal axis is the partial pressure of oxygen in kilopascals, from 0 to 14. The vertical axis is percentage saturation of haemoglobin, from 0 to 100.
The adult curve is S-shaped (sigmoid): flat at low partial pressure, steep in the middle, and levelling off near 97% at the partial pressure in the lungs (about 13 kPa).

The curve at high carbon dioxide (the Bohr effect) lies to the right of it: at the same partial pressure, haemoglobin is less saturated, so it has given up more oxygen. An arrow at 4 kPa shows the extra oxygen unloaded.
The fetal haemoglobin curve lies to the left: at the same partial pressure it is more saturated, so it can take oxygen from the mother's blood.

Shaded bands mark the partial pressures typical of respiring tissue and of the lungs. Curves are drawn from the Hill equation (n = 2.7) with P50 about 3.6 kPa for adult haemoglobin, 4.4 kPa at high CO₂ and 2.5 kPa for fetal haemoglobin: illustrative values, and real ones vary.

review.notes: Round 1: Bohr shift exaggerated (P50 4.8); now 4.4 kPa and labelled illustrative. Round 2: approve.

bus-supply-demand.title: Equilibrium, and what an increase in demand does
bus-supply-demand.caption: Equilibrium is where the curves cross: P = 20, Q = 60 for the worked example. Below it, at P = 15, buyers want 70 but sellers offer only 50: a shortage of 20 that pushes the price up. If demand increases (D → D₂), price and quantity both rise, to P = 25, Q = 70.
bus-supply-demand.alt: Supply and demand diagram with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal. Demand and supply cross at price 20, quantity 60. Demand shifting right moves equilibrium to price 25, quantity 70.
description: Price is on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis, as is conventional in economics.
The demand curve D (Qd = 100 − 2P) slopes down; the supply curve S (Qs = 20 + 2P) slopes up. They cross at the equilibrium E: price 20, quantity 60.

At a price of 15, quantity demanded (70) is greater than quantity supplied (50): a shortage of 20, shown by a double-headed arrow between the two curves, which pushes the price up towards equilibrium.
A dashed curve D₂ (Qd = 120 − 2P) shows an increase in demand. It crosses supply at E₂: price 25, quantity 70. Both price and quantity have risen.

review.notes: Round 1: phone label clipped; surplus arrow crossed D₂; fixed by showing the shortage at P = 15. Round 2: approve.

chem-br2-bromonium.title: Adding Br₂ to cyclohexene: anti addition through a bromonium ion
chem-br2-bromonium.caption: The approaching π bond polarises Br₂. The π electrons bond to the near bromine, which uses a lone pair to bond to the other carbon, giving a bromonium ion that bridges the top face of the ring (wedges). The top face is blocked, so bromide attacks from the bottom face and that bromine ends up on a hash. The two bromines end up on opposite faces: trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane.
chem-br2-bromonium.alt: Mechanism of bromine adding to cyclohexene: a bromonium ion forms on the top face, bromide opens it from the bottom face, giving trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane.
description: Left: cyclohexene with a bromine molecule above its double bond, polarised δ+ on the near bromine and δ− on the far one. Three curly arrows: from the C=C bond to the near bromine; from a lone pair on that bromine back to the other double-bond carbon; and from the Br–Br bond to the far bromine.

Middle: the bromonium ion. A positively charged bromine bridges the two former double-bond carbons; both of its bonds are drawn as wedges, so it sits on the top face of the ring. A bromide ion approaches the right-hand carbon. A curly arrow goes from a lone pair on bromide to that carbon, and another from that carbon's bond to the bridging bromine back onto the bromine.
Right: trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane. One bromine is on a wedge (top face) and the other on a hash (bottom face): the two bromines added to opposite faces, which is anti addition.

review.notes: Round 1: ethene could not show anti addition; replaced by cyclohexene → trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane with a drawn-trans check. Round 2: approve with a caption wording fix, applied.

chem-hbr-propene.title: Adding HBr to propene
chem-hbr-propene.caption: Step 1: the π electrons attack the δ+ hydrogen and the H–Br bond breaks. chem-sn1-sn2-profiles.title: SN1 and SN2 energy profiles
chem-sn1-sn2-profiles.caption: SN2 has one transition state and no intermediate. SN1 has two transition states with a carbocation intermediate in the valley between them; the first barrier is the highest, so ionisation is the rate-determining step.
chem-sn1-sn2-profiles.alt: Two energy profiles. SN2: a single hump. SN1: two humps with a carbocation intermediate in the dip between them, the first hump higher.
description: Left panel, SN2: energy rises from the reactants to a single transition state, marked with a double dagger, then falls to the products, which are lower in energy than the reactants. The activation energy is marked from the reactants to the top of the hump.

Right panel, SN1: energy rises to a first, higher transition state (ionisation), falls into a shallow dip holding the carbocation intermediate, rises to a second, lower transition state (nucleophile attack), then falls to the products. The activation energy of step 1 is marked; it is the largest barrier, so step 1 is rate-determining.

review.notes: Round 1: labels on curves, no plateaus; fixed. Round 2: products label moved below the curve end.

chem-sn2-mechanism.title: SN2: hydroxide and (R)-2-bromobutane
chem-sn2-mechanism.caption: One concerted step, (R) → (S). The lone pair on hydroxide attacks carbon from the side opposite bromine while the C–Br bond breaks. law-duty-of-care.title: Does a duty of care exist?
law-duty-of-care.caption: After Robinson, start with precedent rather than a three-stage test. Precedent can deny a duty as well as recognise one. Only a genuinely novel situation calls for incremental reasoning by analogy, with the Caparo factors weighed together. Separately, there is generally no duty to protect others from harm caused by third parties or to rescue, unless an exception applies.
law-duty-of-care.alt: Decision tree for whether a duty of care exists in negligence, following Robinson v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire Police, Caparo v Dickman and the omissions rule.
description: Question 1: is the claim that the defendant's own act made the claimant worse off, or, if it is about failing to protect them from harm, does an exception apply (the defendant created the danger, assumed responsibility, or had control of the third party or the source of danger)? If no, there is generally no duty: no general duty to prevent harm caused by third parties or to rescue (Smith v Littlewoods; N v Poole BC).

Question 2: is the situation genuinely novel, with no precedent deciding it? If no, follow the precedent: there is a duty where it recognises one (for example road users, doctor and patient), provided the kind of harm to this claimant was reasonably foreseeable; there is no duty where precedent excludes one (Robinson).

If the situation is novel: develop the law incrementally, by analogy with established categories, weighing reasonable foreseeability of damage, proximity, and whether it is fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty, together rather than as separate gates (Caparo; Robinson).

review.notes: Round 1: REJECTED (not novel ≠ duty exists; omissions branch a dead end; Caparo as sequential gates). Rebuilt to follow Robinson. Round 2: approve; the lesson's own K: line, which contradicted Robinson, was corrected.

maths-transformations.title: Tracking a maximum through two transformations
maths-transformations.caption: Track the key point. y = 3f(x − 1): inside the bracket moves x the opposite way (1 right), outside stretches y as written (× 3): (4, 6) → (5, 18). y = f(2x) − 5: inside halves x, outside moves down 5: (4, 6) → (2, 1).
maths-transformations.alt: Graph of a curve y = f(x) with a maximum at (4, 6), and its transformations y = 3f(x − 1), with maximum at (5, 18), and y = f(2x) − 5, with maximum at (2, 1).
description: Three downward parabolas on one set of axes. The original curve y = f(x) has its maximum at (4, 6).
y = 3f(x − 1) is the curve moved 1 to the right and stretched parallel to the y-axis by scale factor 3: it is three times as tall and its maximum is at (5, 18).
y = f(2x) − 5 is stretched parallel to the x-axis by scale factor ½ (so it is narrower) and translated 5 down: its maximum is at (2, 1).
Arrows run from (4, 6) to each new maximum.

phys-converging-lens.title: Ray diagrams for a converging lens
phys-converging-lens.caption: A lens with f = 10 cm. Use the ray rules: a ray parallel to the axis passes through F; a ray through the centre is undeviated; a ray through F emerges parallel. Where they meet is the image. At 2F the image is real, inverted and the same size; inside F the rays diverge and only appear to come from a virtual, upright, magnified image.
phys-converging-lens.alt: Three ray diagrams for a converging lens of focal length 10 cm: object beyond 2F, object at 2F, and object inside F.
description: Each panel shows the principal axis, a converging lens drawn as a vertical double-headed arrow, and the focal points F and 2F on both sides. The lens has focal length 10 cm.
Object beyond 2F (30 cm away): the rays meet 15 cm beyond the lens, forming a real, inverted, diminished image.
Object at 2F (20 cm away): the rays meet at 2F on the other side, forming a real, inverted image the same size as the object.

Object inside F (6 cm away): the rays spread out after the lens. Traced backwards (dashed), they meet 15 cm in front of the lens on the object's side, forming a virtual, upright image 2.5 times larger. This is a magnifying glass.

phys-fbd-slope.title: Box pushed up a rough slope by a horizontal force
phys-fbd-slope.caption: Four forces, each with a physical source. Weight acts from the centre of mass straight down; the normal force is perpendicular to the slope; friction acts down the slope, opposing the motion; the push P is horizontal. Because P presses the box into the slope, N is bigger than mg here: resolving perpendicular to the slope gives N = mg cos θ + P sin θ.
phys-fbd-slope.alt: Free-body diagram of a box on a slope at angle theta, with weight down, normal force perpendicular to the slope, friction down the slope and a horizontal push.
description: A right-angled slope rising to the right at angle theta, with a box resting on it.

Weight, mg, is drawn straight down from the box's centre of mass. The normal force, N, is drawn from the contact face, perpendicular to the slope, pointing away from it. Friction, f, is drawn along the contact face, pointing down the slope. The push, P, is a horizontal arrow arriving at the box from the left.

Because P is horizontal, part of it presses the box into the slope, so the normal force is bigger than mg cos theta: N = mg cos theta + P sin theta. With m = 2 kg, P = 15 N and theta = 25 degrees, N is about 24 N against a weight of about 20 N, and the arrows are drawn to that scale (friction's size is illustrative).

review.notes: Round 1: N drawn shorter than mg, an acceleration note with no arrow; fixed (arrows to scale for m = 2 kg, P = 15 N). Round 2: approve.

phys-kirchhoff-loop.title: Two opposing cells in one loop
phys-kirchhoff-loop.caption: Go round the loop: the 6 V cell is a rise, the 2 V cell (facing the other way) is a drop, and the resistance takes the rest. ΣEMF = ΣIR gives 6 − 2 = I × 4, so I = 1 A, driven by the 6 V cell. The 2 V cell has current forced through it backwards, so it is being charged.

Because the current flows into the 2 V cell's positive terminal, that cell is being charged.

chem-nitration.title: Nitration of benzene
chem-nitration.caption: π electrons from the delocalised ring attack the nitronium ion, NO₂⁺, giving the arenium (Wheland) intermediate: the horseshoe shows the delocalisation broken at the sp³ carbon, with the positive charge spread over the other five, which is why this step is slow. chem-sn1-mechanism.title: SN1: hydrolysis of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane
chem-sn1-mechanism.caption: Step 1 is slow: the C–Br bond breaks on its own, leaving a flat tertiary carbocation and bromide. Water attacks the carbocation (step 2), and a second water molecule removes a proton from the oxonium ion (step 3). Only the haloalkane is involved in the slow, rate-determining step, so rate = k[R–X].
chem-sn1-mechanism.alt: SN1 mechanism: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane ionises to a tertiary carbocation, water attacks it, and loss of a proton gives 2-methylpropan-2-ol.
description: Stage 1: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, a central carbon with three methyl groups and a bromine. A curly arrow goes from the C–Br bond to the bromine. The reaction is in water.

Stage 2: the tertiary carbocation, a positive central carbon with three methyl groups in a flat arrangement, and a bromide ion. A curly arrow goes from a lone pair on the oxygen of a water molecule to the positive carbon.

Stage 3: an oxonium ion, the central carbon bonded to an OH₂⁺ group. A curly arrow goes from a lone pair on a second water molecule to one hydrogen of the OH₂⁺ group, and another from that O–H bond onto the oxygen.
Stage 4: 2-methylpropan-2-ol, a hydronium ion H₃O⁺ and a bromide ion.
